Expert answer

Kutch Ajrakh

The short answer

Ajrakh works as an elaborate resist block-printing technique: the cloth goes through a series of direct and resist printing and dyeing steps, combining hand block printing with resist dyeing. The tannin in myrobalan penetrates the cotton fibres as an essential pre-mordant, which aids the adhesion of the mordants printed on afterwards. On that treated cloth, the iron in the kut paste, oxidised by the air, binds the tannic acid into a deep, fast chocolate-black, while madder dye links to the alum mordant and develops red where the pa and gach pastes were printed.

The monograph

Kutch Ajrakh is an elaborate resist block-printing technique of direct and resist printing and dyeing, made by Khatri artisans as a double-sided textile. Its tradition is kept up in the Kutch villages of Ajrakhpur, Dhamadka and Khavda, and its process and designs are common to Sindh, where it originated, and to Barmer district of Rajasthan. A traditional piece needs all four colours, blue, black, red and white, and the most highly prized cloths were printed identically on both sides.

One cloth, four chemistries

Traditional ajrakh uses four colours, blue, black, red and white, and a piece needs all four to be called ajrakh.

    Indigo, then air

    Green from the vat, blue in the air: Fig. 1.

  • →

    Blackkalo

    Iron on tannin

    On harde-treated cloth kut turns a deep, fast chocolate-black as the iron in the paste, oxidised by the air, binds the tannic acid.

  • →

    Madder on alum

    The long thin roots of Indian madder, Rubia cordifolia or majeeta, give a dye that binds to the alum mordant and develops red where pa and gach were printed.

  • or

    Whitesafed, dhodo

    Lime keeps it

    Lime in the outline resist discharges alum, so the pa paste must not touch khariyanu areas or no red will develop in the later dyeing. Natural madder roots hold more complex colour compounds than synthetic alizarin, so madder dyeing often leaves a pinkish tinge on the white areas.

The cloth itself

Ajrakh is printed mostly on cotton, in natural dyes; printers buy cotton of 60s to 120s count, by what the cloth will become, and print silk ajrakh to order.

What the colours mean

In Karolia and Buch, vadali or neela is blue, the sky; laal is red, the light of sunset; safed or dhodo is white, the stars; and kalo is black, the dark night.

Sources differ on what the colours mean
The GI application reads ajrakh's palette as the universe, with red for the earth, black for darkness, white for clouds and blue for the universe.

The chemistry

Tannin, iron and alum make the colours hold

Madder and synthetic alizarin both need alum as a mordant to develop red, and lime in the outline resist discharges the alum. The blue that appears in the air in Fig. 1 is followed here to its molecules, with the black and the red. Water rich in alum, tin or chrome brightens the colours, while iron in the water supply dulls and darkens the final result.

Synthetic alizarin and madder: both readings hold

Edwards writes that synthetic alizarin and German indigo are chemically identical to the natural dyestuffs. The GI journal finds the colour compounds of natural madder roots much more complex than those of synthetic alizarin, so madder often leaves a pinkish tinge on the whites. Madder holds alizarin and also purpurin, as the GI records for Bagru and Sanganeri prints state.

Blue, from leaf to fibre

Unlike most natural dyes, indigo needs no mordant to hold on the cloth. With Tyrian purple it is one of the natural vat dyes; woad, named beside them, is another plant that gives the same indigo. Tyrian purple is itself an indigo: 6,6′-dibromoindigo, C16H8Br2N2O2, indigo with two bromine atoms. The vat makes it soluble, and on the fibre, in the air, it turns insoluble again.

Where the blue comes from, and back

  1. 1In the leaf

    Indigo plants hold colourless indican, which the enzyme beta-glucosidase turns into colourless indoxyl that oxidises in air to indigo dye.

    Fig. 4, step 1

    Balanced, each indigo is two indoxyl joined, and the leaf’s indican gives up a glucose. Inferred

    From the formulas: indican, PubChem CID 441564; indoxyl, CID 50591; glucose, CID 5793; indigo, CID 10215.

  2. 2Leaf to cake

    Leaves are soaked and churned until they froth blue; the blue paste is filtered, pressed into cakes and dried.

  3. 3Natural or German

    Ajrakh indigo is either natural indigo from Indigofera tinctoria or a synthesised substitute known as German indigo.

  4. 4In the vat

    Fig. 4, step 3

    Traditional vats reduce the dye by fermentation, with naturally occurring microbes under alkaline, anaerobic conditions. Synthetic indigo is set in a clay maat with sodium hydrosulphite and caustic soda for 3 to 4 days.

    The hydros vat, balanced

    C16H10N2O2indigo+Na2S2O4hydros+4 NaOHcaustic soda→C16H10N2Na2O2leucoindigo, as its sodium salt+2 Na2SO3sulfite+2 H2O

    Each side: C 16 · H 14 · N 2 · Na 6 · O 10 · S 2

    The sources name the reagents, sodium hydrosulphite and caustic soda. Balanced, each dithionite gives up two electrons as it becomes two sulfites, and the alkali holds leucoindigo as its soluble sodium salt. Inferred

  5. 5On the cloth

    On the cloth, leucoindigo reoxidises to insoluble blue in air. See Fig. 1

  6. 6Round and back

    In air, indigo white turns to indigo blue, which fermentation must reduce again to soluble indigo white before dyeing can begin.

The source’s own words for step 2

A formula-complete step that does not balance is shown, not hidden, with the hypothesis mark.

Hypothesis

C8H7NOindoxyl+airas the source words it→C16H10N2O2indigo

Carbon 8 before, 16 after: the formulas do not balance, so this is not drawn as a reaction. Fig. 3 shows the balanced form, two indoxyl and one oxygen.

Red, the alum–alizarin lake

Mordant dyes form complexes with metal mordants, and most give different shades with different mordants. With a red dye such as madder or chay root, an alum mordant gives red and an iron mordant gives black. Indian madder holds high amounts of alizarin, the main compound behind red in most natural dyes; alizarin still needs a mordant such as alum to attach to cotton. Edwards writes that the synthetic form of madder is alizarin, chemically identical to the natural dyestuff but far cheaper. Sources differ on how much alizarin Indian madder holds: the GI records for Bagru and Sanganeri name purpurin beside it, and the Met finds India’s red dyes chemically different from dyer’s madder.

The dye is extracted from these long thin roots of Indian madder, which ajrakh has traditionally used, and it links to the alum mordant on the cotton.

Black, iron on tannin

Myrobalan, or harde, a strong tannin from the fruit of the chebulic myrobalan tree, has traditionally been used as a mordant in India. Frater names the dyes of ajrakh's colours as indigo, madder and iron acetate.

The vat, up close

The model drew this explainer from the five cited sentences beneath it while the answer was written, because Model-built explainers was on in Ask. It runs in its own sealed frame, in the fonts that frame can use.

Built from these cited sentences

  1. Traditional indigo vats reduce the dye by fermentation, carried out by naturally occurring microbes under alkaline, anaerobic conditions.
  2. Indigo is transformed to leucoindigo by indigo-reducing bacteria; indigo is not soluble in water, leucoindigo is.
  3. Reduced, the dye is pale yellow and soluble, with an affinity for the fibre.
  4. Leucoindigo penetrates textiles dipped in the fermentation fluid, followed by a brief exposure to air to oxidise it.
  5. Cloth lifted from the indigo vat is bright green at first and turns blue as oxygen meets the dye on the fibres.

The GI journal lists ajrakh’s ingredients as water, harda, scrap iron, tamarisk galls, casatoria seeds, sajikhar salt, madder, alizarin, alum, turmeric, dried pomegranate, jaggery, tamarind seed powder and indigo.

Why Kachchh

When the river died and the iron rose

The GI application states that ajrakh work went on at Dhamadka for the past 450 years because a stream of the Indus gave it water.

The Great Rann of Kachchh: salt flat, not sea, and not Dhamadka or Ajrakhpur. Photo: Ranjith Kumar Inbasekaran, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

“The Dhamadka River was the only one in Kachchh that used to flow in the opposite direction. Usually the rivers originated in the Banni grasslands and flowed southwards. This one would empty itself into the Banni.”

Khamir, Khatris & Community, “Voices across Kachchh: Dhamadka”

History and trade

From Sindh to Kutch at a king’s invitation

The origin of ajrakh can be traced to Sind, now in Pakistan, from where the printing came to Kutch. Ajrakh artisans belong to the Khatri community, Hindu and Muslim, and most artisans of Kutch and Barmer believe their ancestors came from Sindh.

Market, protection and choices

From barter with herders to running yardage

Kutch Ajrakh is an elaborate resist block-printing technique built on a series of direct and resist printing and dyeing steps.

  • 1GI Journal No. 188: Kutch Ajrakh, 2023
  • 2Ajrakh: Rhythm of Blues

Cloth for milk, animals and grain

Khatri printers knew their clients through hereditary relationships and bartered their dyed cloth directly with them for milk, animals and grain.

Muslim Maldhari cattle herders, the traditional purchasers of ajrakh in Kutch, wore it as a lower wrap, a turban and a shoulder cloth.

Rs 7

An ajrakh piece in Barmer, 1975.

40–50

Khatri families printing ajrakh in Barmer in the 1970s.

From caste dress to running yardage

Ajrakh was first adapted for soft furnishings in the mid-1970s and quickly became popular in urban India.

Dr Ismail Mohamed Khatri, credited with much of ajrakh's revival, was awarded an honorary doctorate by De Montfort University.

Cheaper copies

Khatri printers of Kutch have almost stopped printing ajrakh for Maldharis, who buy cheaper screen-printed cloth in chemical dyes, mostly from Pakistan and from Khavda.

Edwards writes that ajrakh's popularity brings threats from the screen-printing industry centred on Jaipur, which reproduces traditional block prints for a fraction of the cost.

What if

What if the dyer changed one thing?

Three choices the sources describe, each shown with what they say follows.

Fig. 21

Set the vat with

A living vat, a month or months to set

Traditionally a naand is dug into the ground, and indigo and casatoria seeds, kuwadia na beej, are left in its water for months for bacteria to grow; the cloth is then dyed for 10 to 15 minutes.

Clifford records a natural indigo vat of indigo, sagikhar salt, lime, casiatora seed and water, fermented for about one month, sometimes with jaggery.

Sources differ: months, or about one month
Karolia and Buch leave the indigo and seeds in the naand for months. Clifford records about one month.

Indigo itself was grown in small amounts at Dhamadka while its river still ran.

A chemical vat, three to four days

Synthetic indigo is set in a clay maat with sodium hydrosulphite and caustic soda and is left to mature for 3 to 4 days.

Natural indigo has been replaced by synthetic indigo to cut down the time of production, though the processes and the number of stages are still the traditional ones.

Indigo fermentation has been replaced by chemical reduction with sodium dithionite, whose by-products make the dye waste hard to dispose of.

Edwards writes that German indigo is chemically identical to the natural dyestuff but far cheaper, reliable and easy to use.

A hydros vat is ready in 3 to 4 days; a natural vat takes about a month, or months

Days. The hatched span runs between the two sources’ readings for the natural vat.

C16H10N2O2IndigoPubChem CID 10215
Na2S2O4Sodium hydrosulphite, or sodium dithionitePubChem CID 24489NaOHCaustic sodaPubChem CID 14798C16H10N2O2IndigoPubChem CID 10215

The same in either vat

The dip is the same in either vat: Fig. 1.

For the darkest blues the cloth may be dipped three or four times in the indigo vat, and it is reprinted between dips when two blue shades are wanted.

Dye the red with

Madder root: red, with a pink cast on the whites

Indian madder’s long thin roots give the red, binding to the alum mordant where pa and gach were printed.

Natural madder roots hold more complex colour compounds than synthetic alizarin, so madder dyeing often leaves a pinkish tinge on the white areas.

Tapano bleached that tinge: the cloth was soaked in camel dung and kept moist on sandy river banks for at least three days.

Synthetic alizarin: the dye that replaced madder

First made in a laboratory in 1868: the 1868 entry of Fig. 18.

Despite being synthetic, alizarin still needs a mordant such as alum to attach its colour to the cotton fibres.

C14H8O4AlizarinPubChem CID 6293C14H8O5PurpurinPubChem CID 6683KAl(SO4)2·12H2OPotassium alumKalaVigyan compound library

One molecule, or a mixture

Edwards writes that synthetic alizarin is chemically identical to the natural dyestuff but far cheaper, reliable and easy to use.

Madder root carries more than alizarin: the Bagru GI journal names alizarin and purpurin in it, and says synthetic alizarin is used because vegetable alizarin is short.

If the pa paste touches the lime outline, the lime discharges the alum and no red develops there.

No red where the pa met lime

Day 0 of 3 in the sun
Let the pa touch the lime outlineWhat the GI journal warns against

The red bath: 2 to 3 hours, or up to 4 for the purest reds

Hours. The hatched span is where the two sources disagree.

Wash the myrobalan-yellow cloth in

Alum, tin or chrome in the water: brighter colours

Alum, tin or chrome in the water brightens ajrakh colours.

Printers wash early in the morning, because warmer afternoon water may dissolve some of the alum.

Iron in the water: dull colours and black spots

Even one percent of iron in the wash water leaves black spots on pale yellow, myrobalan-dyed cloth, an artisan explained to Mongabay.

At Ajrakhpur excess iron is again among the threats to the craft, with a falling water table and rising salinity.

उत्तरविशेषज्ञ44 स्रोतों सेA 28B 11C 5Kutch Ajrakh मोनोग्राफउत्तर दिया 18 नवंबर 2026

Ajrakh एक विस्तृत प्रतिरोध (रेज़िस्ट) ब्लॉक-छपाई तकनीक है: कपड़ा सीधी और प्रतिरोध छपाई तथा रँगाई के कई चरणों से गुज़रता है, जिनमें हाथ की ब्लॉक छपाई और प्रतिरोध रँगाई एक साथ चलती हैं। हरड़ (मायरोबालन) का टैनिन एक आवश्यक पूर्व-रंगबंधक के रूप में सूती रेशों में समा जाता है, जिससे बाद में छापे जाने वाले रंगबंधक कपड़े पर चिपकते हैं। इस उपचारित कपड़े पर kut लेप का लोहा टैनिक अम्ल के साथ ऑक्सीकृत होकर गहरा, पक्का चॉकलेटी-काला रंग देता है, जबकि मजीठ का रंग फिटकरी के रंगबंधक से जुड़कर वहाँ लाल उभारता है जहाँ Pa और Gach लेप छापे गए थे।

रसायन

टैनिन, लोहा और फिटकरी रंगों को पक्का करते हैं

हरड़ में टैनिक अम्ल की मात्रा अधिक होती है; यह एक आवश्यक पूर्व-रंगबंधक है जो छापे गए रंगबंधकों को सूती कपड़े पर चिपकने में मदद करता है। हरड़ से उपचारित कपड़े पर छापा गया kut गहरा, पक्का चॉकलेटी-काला हो जाता है, क्योंकि लेप का लोहा टैनिक अम्ल के साथ ऑक्सीकृत होता है। लाल रंग उभारने के लिए मजीठ और संश्लेषित एलिज़ारिन, दोनों को रंगबंधक के रूप में फिटकरी चाहिए, और रूपरेखा के प्रतिरोध-लेप का चूना फिटकरी को हटा देता है। नील के कुंड से निकाला गया कपड़ा चटक हरा होता है और रेशों पर रंग से ऑक्सीजन के मिलते ही नीला हो जाता है।

جوابماہر44 ذرائع سےA 28B 11C 5Kutch Ajrakh مونوگرافجواب دیا گیا 18 نومبر 2026

Ajrakh ایک مفصل مزاحم ٹھپا چھپائی کی تکنیک ہے: کپڑا براہِ راست اور مزاحم چھپائی اور رنگائی کے کئی مرحلوں سے گزرتا ہے، جن میں ہاتھ کی ٹھپا چھپائی اور مزاحم رنگائی یکجا ہوتی ہیں۔ ہڑ کا ٹینن ایک لازمی ابتدائی رنگ بند کے طور پر سوتی ریشوں میں جذب ہو جاتا ہے، جس سے بعد میں چھاپے جانے والے رنگ بند کپڑے پر جمتے ہیں۔ اس تیار شدہ کپڑے پر kut لیپ کا لوہا ٹینک ایسڈ کے ساتھ تکسید ہو کر گہرا، پکا چاکلیٹی سیاہ رنگ دیتا ہے، جبکہ مجیٹھ کا رنگ پھٹکری کے رنگ بند سے جڑ کر وہاں سرخی ابھارتا ہے جہاں Pa اور Gach لیپ چھاپے گئے تھے۔

کیمیا

ٹینن، لوہا اور پھٹکری رنگوں کو پکا کرتے ہیں

ہڑ میں ٹینک ایسڈ کی مقدار زیادہ ہوتی ہے؛ یہ ایک لازمی ابتدائی رنگ بند ہے جو چھاپے گئے رنگ بندوں کو سوتی کپڑے پر جمنے میں مدد دیتا ہے۔ ہڑ سے تیار کیے گئے کپڑے پر چھاپا گیا kut گہرا، پکا چاکلیٹی سیاہ ہو جاتا ہے، کیونکہ لیپ کا لوہا ٹینک ایسڈ کے ساتھ تکسید ہوتا ہے۔ سرخ رنگ ابھارنے کے لیے مجیٹھ اور مصنوعی ایلیزرین، دونوں کو بطور رنگ بند پھٹکری درکار ہے، اور خاکے کے مزاحم لیپ کا چونا پھٹکری کو ہٹا دیتا ہے۔ نیل کے حوض سے نکالا گیا کپڑا شوخ سبز ہوتا ہے اور ریشوں پر رنگ سے آکسیجن ملتے ہی نیلا ہو جاتا ہے۔

Two more ways to read this answer

The student versionFor a reader of 14 to 17 · open to read

Student, 14 to 17

The cloth is dipped in the dye vat, then taken out into the air. There the dye turns back from indigo white into blue indigo. Blue indigo does not dissolve, and it holds fast to the cotton. Why a vat? Indigo will not dissolve in water. Bacteria in the vat turn it into leucoindigo, which does. The cloth comes out bright green. Then oxygen in the air reaches the dye and turns it blue.

Answer written7 sections, 7 illustrations, 1 video and the film

Illustrate as I writePictures, a short video and a film of this answer, each labelled AI.
1

Tannin, iron and alum make the colours hold

ChemistryWritten

Myrobalan contains high levels of tannic acid, an essential pre-mordant that aids the adhesion of the printed mordants onto the cotton. Printed on harde-treated cloth, kut develops a deep fast chocolate-black as the iron in the paste, oxidised by the air, binds the tannic acid. Madder and synthetic alizarin both need alum as a mordant to develop red, and lime in the outline resist discharges the alum.

2

From Sindh to Kutch at a king's invitation

HistoryWritten

The origin of ajrakh is traced to Sind, and Rao Bharmalji I of Kutch invited Khatri printers from Sindh and gave them land and freedom from tax. Many Khatri printers descend from Jindha Jiva, who founded Dhamadka in the reign of Rao Bharmal I, and Dhamadka and Khavda became the main centres of ajrakh in Kachchh. Indian cotton fragments of the 11th to 14th century found at Al Fustat in Old Cairo were printed with small blocks in simple patterns that bear a striking similarity to ajrak.

3

Blue, red, black and white, printed both sides

OverviewWritten

Kutch Ajrakh is an elaborate resist block-printing technique of direct and resist printing and dyeing, made by Khatri artisans as a double-sided textile. Its tradition is kept up in the Kutch villages of Ajrakhpur, Dhamadka and Khavda, and its process and designs are common to Sindh, where it originated, and to Barmer district of Rajasthan. A traditional piece needs all four colours, blue, black, red and white, and the most highly prized cloths were printed identically on both sides.

4

When the river died and the iron rose

Geography and waterWritten

Edwards writes that the River Suran served Dhamadka until the late 1980s, and the GI journal records that its water stream dried up in 1989. After the 2001 earthquake Dhamadka's water held more iron, which saddens dye colours, and even one percent of iron leaves black spots on myrobalan-dyed cloth. Ajrakhpur was chosen for good quality groundwater, but its water table is going down and excess iron and rising salinity threaten the craft again.

5

From barter with herders to running yardage

EconomicsWritten

Khatri printers knew their clients through hereditary relationships and bartered their dyed cloth directly with them for milk, animals and grain. Khatri printers of Kutch have almost stopped printing ajrakh for Maldharis, who buy cheaper screen-printed cloth in chemical dyes, mostly from Pakistan and from Khavda. In 2014 Abduljabbar M. Khatri's workshop made 70,000 m of running cotton yardage for Fabindia, one of his largest clients with Maiwa.

6

Balance, order and the priest-king's cloud motif

DesignWritten

Ajrakh design follows mizan, the Islamic principle of balance and order, with the design square divided into quarters and then sixteen parts. A fixed layout sets a large central body of a repeated motif on a tight grid within borders and end panels. Block printers identify the trefoil on the Mohenjo-daro priest-king's shawl with kakar, the cloud motif of ajrakh.

7

Camel dung, myrobalan and lime prepare the cloth

ProcessWritten

The cloth is first scoured in saaj by repeated soaking in castor oil, soda ash and camel dung and drying until it is soft and white, though sources differ on whether these ingredients are still used. In kasanu it is treated with harda (myrobalan), and the white outlines are then printed with rekh blocks in a resist of gum arabic and lime. Kat prints the black with an iron paste, and kan or pa prints a paste of alum and tamarind seed powder where red is required.
